rationale: The defined notion is verbatim standard: the topology of pointwise convergence on Y^X is the product topology on the product of X copies of Y, equivalently the initial topology of the evaluation projections, with basic open sets constraining finitely many coordinates. Munkres, Topology 2nd ed., Sec. 46 introduces it under exactly this name and identification. The item adds nothing to the sourced content; the subspace restriction to C(X,Y) is the standard subspace construction. Definition, so no proof component.

The statement 'f_k -> f in the product/pointwise topology iff f_k(x) -> f(x) for every x' is the standard fact that names the topology, stated in the sourced articles with the same hypotheses, direction and quantifiers (no uniqueness of limits asserted). Convention delta: none. The local proof, including the choice-free handling of the finite maximum over indices, is written for this library; I verified the argument but did not locate a source proof, so the proof component is recorded as locally invented.

Munkres Sec. 29 defines: 'A topological space X is locally compact at point x if there is some compact subspace [K] of X that contains a neighborhood of x. If X is locally compact at each of its points, [X] is locally compact.' The item is that condition specialised to a metric space and unwound into ball form (there are a compact K and a real r > 0 with B(x,r) subset of K). Convention deltas: (a) restricted to metric spaces, since the library's only compactness notion for subsets at this point is def-metric-compactness; (b) the neighbourhood is written as a ball, which the item itself proves equivalent; (c) neighbourhoods are not required to be open, as in the source. Same content, reformulated and specialised, hence ai-altered rather than exact.

The standard result is that in a locally compact Hausdorff space every point has a neighbourhood base of compact sets (Wikipedia, Locally compact space; Munkres Sec. 29). The item is that statement specialised to a metric space and sharpened to the concrete family of small CLOSED BALLS: there is r_0 > 0 with every closed ball of radius r in (0,r_0) compact, and those balls a neighbourhood base at x. Convention delta: the source gives compact neighbourhoods abstractly, the item names closed balls and the threshold r_0, which is the metric specialisation. Local proof.

Munkres Lemma 26.8 (The Tube Lemma): 'Consider the product space X x Y where Y is compact. If N is an open set of X x Y containing the slice {x_0} x Y of X x Y, then N contains some tube W x Y about {x_0} x Y, where W is a neighborhood of x_0 in X.' The item states the same content with three deltas: the two factors are transposed (the compact factor is written first), the compact factor is a compact SUBSET K of a metric space X rather than a whole compact factor, and X is metric. The subset form is the routine relativisation of the source and the empty case is settled explicitly by W := Z. Local proof, deliberately indexed by pairs to stay choice-free.

Verbatim: 'Given a compact subset K of X and an open subset U of Y, let V(K,U) denote the set of all functions f in C(X,Y) such that f(K) is a subset of U ... the collection of all such V(K,U) is a subbase for the compact-open topology on C(X,Y).' The item's S(K,V) is that set and that subbasis, with identical hypotheses on K and V and the same generated topology. Convention delta (scope only, not content): X is a metric space here because def-metric-compactness is the library's only compactness notion for subsets at this point; the defining condition is unchanged. Definition, so no proof component; the degenerate identities S(empty,V) = S(K,Y) = C(X,Y) are immediate unfoldings.

This is Munkres's uniform metric, not a new object in the literature. Munkres Sec. 20: 'rho(x,y) = sup{ d-bar(x_a,y_a) } where d-bar(x_a,y_a) = min{|x_a - y_a|,1} is the standard bounded metric ... Metric rho-bar is the uniform metric on R^J and the metric topology it induces is the uniform topology'; Munkres Sec. 43 generalises verbatim to a metric target: 'rho-bar is the uniform metric on Y^J corresponding to d', with rho-bar(f,g) = sup{ d-bar(f(a),g(a)) : a in J }. Same formula, same truncation at 1, same claim that it is a metric. Convention delta: the item states X nonempty explicitly, which the source leaves implicit in its sup; this is a scope precision forced by rem-sup-conventions (no extended real line), not a content change. IMPORTANT for readers of this item's own Remark: 'new' there means new RELATIVE TO THIS LIBRARY's lem-sup-metric-is-a-metric, not new to mathematics; the statement is sourced and must not be read as ai-generated. Local proof.

Two sourced notions, both verbatim. (i) Uniform convergence: for every real epsilon > 0 there is K with d(f_k(x),f(x)) < epsilon for every x and every k >= K, one index serving every point. (ii) 'the metric topology it induces is the uniform topology' (Munkres Sec. 20), the metric being the uniform metric of Sec. 43. The subspace reading on C(X,Y) is the standard subspace construction and the item discharges its agreement with the subspace-metric topology. Convention delta: X nonempty, inherited from the uniform metric. Definition, no proof component.

That convergence in the uniform metric is exactly uniform convergence is the standard fact justifying the name of the topology, and it is what Munkres Sec. 20/43 assert when they call rho-bar's topology the uniform topology; the sourced relation rho-bar(f,g) = min{rho(f,g),1} in the Sec. 43 note is the same truncation observation the item uses. Same direction (a biconditional), same hypotheses. Local proof; the threshold argument pushing eta below 1 is written here.

The topology of compact convergence (uniform convergence on compact sets) with basic sets B_K(f,epsilon) = {g : d(f(x),g(x)) < epsilon for every x in K} is the standard definition, Munkres Sec. 46; the sourced characterisation 'a sequence {f_n} converges to f in the compact-open topology if and only if for every compact subset K of X, {f_n} converges uniformly to f on K' is the same notion. Convention delta: the item deliberately writes the pointwise condition rather than a supremum, so that K = empty is harmless in a library with no sup of the empty set. Proof recorded as ai-generated rather than not-applicable because this definition carries substantive local verification: the basis conditions (B1)/(B2) and the three auxiliary facts (U1) union of two compacta, (U2) continuity of x |-> d(f(x),g(x)), (U3) attainment of the maximum on a nonempty compact set, plus (U4) the neighbourhood base at f.

Sourced verbatim: 'if Y is a metric space (or more generally, a uniform space), then the compact-open topology is equal to the topology of compact convergence.' The item narrows that to a metric DOMAIN as well as a metric target, because compact subsets of X are available here only through def-metric-compactness. Convention delta: an added hypothesis on X, no change to the conclusion or direction. Semantically the same theorem, specialised, hence ai-altered. Local proof; both halves written here, the first through the extreme value theorem applied to the distance to Y minus V, the second by a covering argument indexed by pairs.

The chain 'pointwise coarser than compact convergence coarser than uniform' on C(X,Y) is the standard comparison of Munkres Sec. 46, stated there for a metric target and an arbitrary topological domain. The item narrows the domain to a nonempty metric space (nonemptiness inherited from the uniform metric, metricity from compactness of subsets). Same two inclusions, same direction, no strictness claimed on either side, matching the source. Added hypotheses only, hence ai-altered. Local proof.

Claim 2 is Munkres Theorem 21.6 verbatim, including its exact hypotheses: 'Let f_n : X -> Y be a sequence of continuous functions from the topological space X to the metric space Y. If {f_n} converges uniformly to f, then f is continuous.' Claim 3 is the first sentence of Munkres Theorem 43.6 verbatim: 'The set C(X,Y) of continuous functions is closed in Y^X under the uniform metric', for X a topological space and (Y,d) a metric space. Claim 1, the epsilon/3 criterion, is the standard uniform-approximation criterion that the textbook proof of 21.6 runs on, stated here as a separate claim. No hypothesis added or dropped. Local proof; claim 3 is deliberately routed around thm-metric-sequential-closure to stay in ZF, which is a local design choice rather than the source's route.

Claim 1 is Munkres Theorem 43.5 verbatim: 'If the space Y is complete in the metric d, then the space Y^J is complete in the uniform metric rho-bar corresponding to d.' Claim 2 is the closing sentence of Munkres Theorem 43.6 verbatim: 'if Y is a complete metric space, then both C(X,Y) and B(X,Y) are complete metric spaces under the uniform metric.' Convention delta: X nonempty, inherited from the uniform metric and implicit in the source. Local proof; the limit function is defined by a formula and step 4.1 instantiates an index inside one sentence, both to keep the argument choice-free.

Verbatim from the sourced article: 'the evaluation map e : C(X,Y) x X -> Y, defined by e(f,x) = f(x)'. The item fixes the same map with the same domain, the same product topology on the source and the compact-open topology on C(X,Y) as the standing convention. Convention delta: factor order (the sourced nLab statement writes ev : X x Y^X -> Y); the item records the swap explicitly and notes it is immaterial. Definition, no proof component; the separate-continuity observations are one-line unfoldings.

Sourced verbatim: 'if X is a locally compact Hausdorff (or preregular) space, then the evaluation map e : C(X,Y) x X -> Y, defined by e(f,x) = f(x), is continuous' (Wikipedia); nLab's Proposition (evIsContinuous) states it with local compactness alone. The item narrows X to a locally compact METRIC space, which is a specialisation of both forms (a metric space is Hausdorff, so the Hausdorff hypothesis is discharged rather than dropped) and imposes no hypothesis on Y, as in the sources. Added hypothesis only, hence ai-altered. Local proof.

nLab Proposition (alphafIsContinuous): 'Let (X,O_X), (Y,O_Y), and (Z,O_Z) be topological spaces. Let f : X x Y -> Z be a continuous map ... Then the map alpha_f : X -> Z^Y ... is continuous ... where Z^Y is equipped with the compact-open topology', with NO hypothesis on the exponent space. This is Munkres Theorem 46.11's easy half. The item states exactly that, with the single delta that its X (the compactness-carrying factor) is metric, because compact subsets are available here only for metric spaces. Same conclusion, same direction, one added hypothesis, hence ai-altered. Local proof, through the metric tube lemma.

The sourced statement is stronger: nLab's Corollary (GivesExponentialObject) says that for X locally compact, Y^X with the compact-open topology and ev is an EXPONENTIAL OBJECT in Top, and Wikipedia says 'if X is locally compact, then X x - from the category of topological spaces always has a right adjoint Hom(X,-)'. The item deliberately claims only the underlying BIJECTION between C(X x Z,Y) and C(Z,C(X,Y)), with X locally compact metric, and states in terms that it is not claiming a homeomorphism. So the item is the sourced result weakened in its conclusion and narrowed in its hypothesis on X. Both deltas are recorded on the item itself. Weakening plus specialisation, hence ai-altered. Local proof. SEE FINDING F1: the item's second Remark gives a reason for the weakening that the library's current contents falsify.

All three notions are sourced verbatim in the item's own metric epsilon-delta form. Wikipedia, Equicontinuity: 'The family F is equicontinuous at a point x_0 in X if for every epsilon > 0, there exists a delta > 0 such that d(f(x_0), f(x)) < epsilon for all f in F and all x such that d(x_0, x) < delta'; and 'The family F is uniformly equicontinuous if for every epsilon > 0, there exists a delta > 0 such that d(f(x_1), f(x_2)) < epsilon for all f in F and all x_1, x_2 in X such that d(x_1,x_2) < delta.' Munkres Sec. 45 gives pointwise boundedness verbatim: 'a subset F of C(X,Y) is pointwise bounded under d if for each a in X, the subset F_a = {f(a) | f in F} of Y is bounded under d.' No hypothesis, quantifier or direction changed. Definition, no proof component.

Sourced statement: X a compact TOPOLOGICAL space, (f_n) a monotonically increasing sequence of continuous real-valued functions converging pointwise to a continuous f : X -> R; then the convergence is uniform, and the monotonically decreasing form holds too. The item is that statement with X specialised to a compact METRIC space, the monotonicity written out pointwise as f_k(x) <= f_{k+1}(x), and the nonincreasing form recorded as a consequence of applying the theorem to the negatives rather than proved separately. Added hypothesis and reformulation only; conclusion and direction unchanged. Local proof, kept choice-free by taking the finite subcover as a list of indices.

Positive determination of novelty: this is a page-conventions remark about THIS LIBRARY's standing hypotheses, notation, reading order and scope. It has no counterpart in the mathematical literature and could not have one, so it is genuinely locally authored rather than merely unsourced. No load-bearing mathematical claim is made and no item depends on it (verified: zero reverse-deps corpus-wide), so the ai-generated statement label creates no dependency-eligibility problem. Follows the established retro-tag precedent for conventions remarks in this corpus (rem-topology-conventions, rem-counting-conventions-and-scope, rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric, rem-constructions-this-page-stops-short-of, rem-sieve-pigeonhole-and-double-counting-conventions, rem-complete-metrizability-is-the-topological-shadow), all tagged ai-generated with no generation block. Truth-risk check performed: SEE FINDING F1, which reports two false clauses in section 1 of this remark.

The refuted claim is the standard warning that pointwise convergence does not imply uniform convergence, recorded in the sourced articles, here sharpened to the compact-convergence form. The witness is the classical moving spike on [0,1]: continuous piecewise-linear tents of height 1 with support shrinking to 0, the standard textbook counterexample (Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis 3rd ed., Ch. 7). Convention deltas: the spike is indexed on a_k = 1/(k+2) because N contains 0 here, and the conclusion is phrased against the topology of compact convergence rather than against uniform convergence directly. Established witness reformulated to this library's indexing, hence ai-altered, not a bespoke invention. Local refutation.

Non-metrizability of the compact-open topology in general is standard, and every ingredient of the witness is standard: on a discrete domain the compact sets are exactly the finite sets, so the compact-open topology coincides with the product topology; and an uncountable product of nontrivial spaces, here R^R, is not first countable, while a metrizable space is first countable. The composition into a single named witness (R with the discrete metric) is a routine assembly of sourced facts rather than an invented claim, hence ai-altered rather than ai-generated. Local refutation, which correctly flags at step 9.1 that the Axiom of Countable Choice is spent once, in the countable union of the finite sets G_k.

The sourced positive theorem carries local compactness as a hypothesis ('if X is a locally compact Hausdorff space, then the evaluation map ... is continuous'), and Q is the standard example of a metric space that is locally compact at no point (Munkres Sec. 29, Exercise 29.1: 'you will show that Q is not locally compact'). The refuted claim is the sourced theorem with its hypothesis deleted, and the witness is the standard one. The explicit bump function g(s) = (2/eta) d(s,A) used to force the contradiction is a routine Lipschitz construction from lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz, not a novel object. Hence ai-altered. Local refutation.

Every claim is sourced and the item is their worked instance on [0,1]. Completeness of C(I,R) in the uniform metric is Munkres Theorem 43.6. The relation between the two metrics is the Munkres Sec. 43 note, verbatim in content: 'In either case, we have rho-bar(f,g) = min{rho(f,g),1}', which is exactly why they are uniformly equivalent below the threshold; boundedness of every continuous function on a compact interval is the extreme value theorem. Specialisation and merging of sourced results into one worked example, hence ai-altered. Local verification.

The moving spike is the classical witness (Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis 3rd ed., Ch. 7) and the three assertions traced here (pointwise convergence, uniform distance identically 1, no convergence in compact convergence) are the standard readings of it. What is local is only the tracing through this page's three named topologies and the library's index shift to a_k = 1/(k+2). Established witness reformulated, hence ai-altered. Local verification.

That compact convergence is strictly coarser than uniform convergence on a non-compact domain is standard, and g_k(x) = x/(k+1) on R is the standard separating family: it converges to 0 uniformly on every bounded set and has uniform distance 1 from 0 for every k, the discrepancy escaping to x = k+1. Convention delta: the index shift to iota(k+1) because N contains 0. Established witness reformulated, hence ai-altered. Local verification.

Three sourced facts specialised to C(R,R): the compact subsets of R are the closed bounded ones so the intervals [-m,m] exhaust them (Heine-Borel); the compact-open topology equals compact convergence for a metric target, whose sets B_K(f,epsilon) centred at f are a neighbourhood base; and R is locally compact (Munkres Sec. 29, Example 1: 'R is locally compact since x in R lies in neighborhood (x-1,x+1) which is in the compact space [x-1,x+1]'), so evaluation is continuous. Specialisation and merging of sourced results, hence ai-altered. Local verification.

Claim 1 is sourced verbatim: 'A set of functions with a common Lipschitz constant is (uniformly) equicontinuous.' Claim 2, that x |-> d(x,A) is 1-Lipschitz for nonempty A, is the standard property of the distance function and is lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz in this library. Claim 3, that the family is not pointwise bounded because it contains every constant, is a one-line check on the sourced family. The item is the bundling of these three into one example with an explicit named family L, hence ai-altered rather than exact. Local verification.

That pointwise boundedness and equicontinuity are independent hypotheses is the standard reading of the Ascoli-Arzela theorem, whose statement carries both (Munkres Theorem 45.4: 'A subspace F of C(X,R^n) has compact closure if and only if F is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded under d'), and the spike family with values in [0,1] and unbounded slopes is the classical witness for the failing direction (Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis 3rd ed., Ch. 7). What is local is the reuse of this page's own already-built spikes. Established witness reformulated, hence ai-altered. Local verification.

That a pointwise limit of continuous functions need not be continuous is the standard contrast drawn by the sourced articles against the uniform limit theorem, and the ramp family rising to 1 only at the right endpoint is the classical witness, of the same shape as the textbook t |-> t^n on [0,1] converging to the indicator of {1}. Convention deltas: piecewise-linear ramps rather than powers, and the index shift a_k = 1/(k+2). The pointwise-nonincreasing observation is added locally so that the family can serve as the Dini failure witness later on the page. Established witness reformulated, hence ai-altered. Local verification.

A worked instance of the sourced exponential law on X = Z = Y = R, with the multiplication map as the chosen f. Multiplication on R x R is continuous, its transpose is the family of multiplication-by-z maps, each Lipschitz with constant |z|, and local compactness of R is Munkres Sec. 29 Example 1. Every ingredient is standard; the composition into one traced example, and the direct estimate |x||z-z_0| <= iota(m)|z-z_0| on [-m,m] replacing the tube lemma, are local. Hence ai-altered. Local verification.

A worked instance of the sourced Dini theorem on [0,1] together with its standard sharpness discussion. The clipped identities s_k(t) = min{t, 1 - a_k} form a nondecreasing sequence of continuous functions converging pointwise to the continuous identity, which is a routine instance rather than a novel construction, and the failure clause reuses this page's ramps to show that continuity of the limit cannot be dropped, which is the standard remark accompanying Dini's theorem. Specialisation of a sourced theorem plus a standard sharpness witness, hence ai-altered. Local verification; note that the positive half is also proved directly by the bound |s_k(t) - t| <= a_k, independent of Dini.
